authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro candidate authoring; human review required

items.prompt: A service map lists direct communication links between services. The question asks whether service T can be reached from service S by following any number of links. What is the decisive problem structure?

options.text: A sorting problem because service names can be ordered alphabetically.
States connected by legal transitions, requiring graph traversal from S.
A binary-search problem because the target service has a known name.
A graph problem only if BFS is used, because BFS is always faster than DFS.

feedback.reason: The answer depends on following a relation from one state to other reachable states, which is the graph-traversal signal.

blocks.text: Reachability follows links transitively

Model each service as a vertex and each followable communication link as an edge. T is reachable from S if T = S or there is a sequence S → … → T of zero or more legal links. A traversal starts at S, expands linked services, and uses visited state so a cycle does not cause repeated processing.

blocks.title: Surface labels do not choose the algorithm
blocks.text: Alphabetically sorting service names or binary-searching a known name can find a record, but neither operation proves that a communication path connects S to T. BFS and DFS are implementation choices after the graph structure is recognized.

blocks.title: Recognition rule
blocks.text: When the answer depends on repeatedly following a relation from one state to another, model states and transitions and ask a graph reachability question.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_services: Alphabetical order does not preserve communication reachability; the links define the relevant structure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_search: Binary search locates a key in an ordered collection; it does not follow arbitrary communication links.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_only: Reachability is the graph signal; BFS and DFS are both valid full traversals when shortest distance is not requested.

items.prompt: A puzzle state is a word. One move changes one character, and only dictionary words are legal. The task asks whether the start word can reach the target word. Which signal identifies the approach family?
constraints: The start and target are dictionary words of the same length.

options.text: It becomes graph traversal only after an adjacency matrix is built.
It is only a string-scanning task because every state is text.
Each legal word is a state and each one-character move is an edge in an implicit graph.
It is graph traversal only if visited states are marked when dequeued.

feedback.reason: Repeated legal transformations create an implicit state graph even though no edge list is provided.

blocks.text: A transition rule can define a graph without an edge file

items: Treat every legal same-length dictionary word as a state.
Generate a neighbor by changing one position to another character and retaining the result only when it is in the dictionary.
Traverse those legal transitions from the start while recording visited words.
Succeed when the target is discovered; fail when the reachable frontier is empty.

blocks.text: The fact that vertices are strings does not make this a one-string scan: the answer depends on a sequence of transformations through many words. An adjacency matrix is optional because neighbors can be generated from the rule. Visited timing affects duplicate work after the graph has already been identified.

blocks.title: Implicit-state signal
blocks.text: Legal objects are vertices and repeatable legal transformations are edges, even when the input never materializes those edges.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.string_scan: The answer depends on sequences of legal transformations, not on a single pass over one string.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_required: A graph can be implicit; legal neighbors may be generated from the transition rule without a matrix.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dequeue_marks_graph: Visited timing is an implementation invariant, not the signal that states and transitions form a graph.

items.prompt: An unweighted transit map gives stations and direct rides. The task asks for the minimum number of rides from A to B. Which feature is decisive?

options.text: Use DFS because it dives to B sooner on average.
Use an adjacency matrix because shortest paths require constant-time edge checks.
Treat the map as a tree and follow parent pointers because routes cannot cycle.
Every ride has equal cost, so distance is the number of graph edges and BFS layers are relevant.

feedback.reason: Equal-cost edges make the requested minimum ride count an unweighted shortest-path traversal problem.

blocks.text: Equal-cost edges turn ride count into BFS depth

BFS starts with A at distance 0, then processes all stations one ride away, then two rides away, and so on. Because every direct ride adds exactly one to the distance, the first time B is discovered its layer number is the minimum possible ride count.

blocks.title: Do not confuse three separate choices
blocks.text: DFS can discover a longer route before a shorter one. A matrix versus a list is a representation decision, and the map is not promised to be a tree. None of those claims establishes minimum edge count.

blocks.title: Transfer boundary
blocks.text: Use BFS layers for minimum edge count when every edge has equal cost; unequal ride costs require a weighted shortest-path method.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dfs_faster: DFS discovery order does not guarantee the fewest edges, and average intuition is not the stated answer contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_density: Representation may vary; the equal edge-cost shortest-path contract is what selects layer-based traversal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tree_path: A transit graph may contain cycles and multiple routes; tree assumptions are not provided.

items.prompt: Tasks have prerequisite pairs, and the output must list every task after all of its prerequisites. Which graph-traversal signal matters most?
constraints: If no legal ordering exists, report that the prerequisite graph contains a directed cycle.

options.text: Any BFS or DFS visitation order is valid because all tasks only need to be reached.
Directed dependencies impose a partial order, so topological processing is required.
Choose BFS because it is always faster than DFS and therefore creates the correct order.
Drop edge directions and treat prerequisites as an undirected tree.

feedback.reason: The output is not merely a reachable set; it must respect directed prerequisite constraints.

blocks.text: The output must satisfy every directed precedence edge

Model prerequisite p for task t as p → t. A legal output is a topological order: for every such edge, p appears before t. Indegree processing repeatedly removes tasks with no remaining prerequisites; DFS postorder is another implementation when it also detects cycles.

blocks.title: Reachability is too weak
blocks.text: An ordinary BFS or DFS order may visit every task yet still place t before prerequisite p. Dropping direction erases the meaning of the constraint, and no ordering can satisfy a directed cycle.

blocks.title: Recognition rule
blocks.text: When every directed dependency must precede its dependent, the required object is a topological order plus explicit cycle handling.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ordinary_reachability: Reachability alone does not guarantee that every prerequisite appears before its dependent task.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fastest_traversal: Runtime preference does not enforce the dependency invariant; both naive visitation orders can violate it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.undirected_tree: Direction carries the prerequisite meaning; removing it destroys the ordering contract and cycles may exist.

items.prompt: An array of integers is given, and the task asks for the maximum sum of one contiguous subarray. No relation between arbitrary indices is defined. Which classification is correct?

options.text: Treat every index as a vertex and adjacent indices as edges, then run BFS.
Build an adjacency matrix of index pairs to avoid missing subarrays.
This is not a graph-traversal signal; the key structure is a contiguous sequence and a running-state decision.
Treat the array as a rooted tree because each index has a next index.

feedback.reason: A graph model is not useful merely because positions can be connected; the decisive invariant is contiguous accumulation.

blocks.text: A possible graph model is not necessarily a useful one

For each value x in scan order, the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray ending at x is either x alone or the previous ending sum plus x. The update `ending = max(x, ending + x)` retains exactly that decision, while a separate maximum records the best ending seen.

Turning adjacent indices into path edges is mathematically possible, but BFS over that path does not compute the accumulation invariant. An adjacency matrix adds irrelevant pair storage, and calling the sequence a tree does not expose the maximum-sum decision.

blocks.title: Reject over-modeling
blocks.text: Choose graph traversal only when connectivity or repeatable state transitions drive the requested output, not merely because objects can be drawn as vertices.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.index_graph: Although any sequence can be modeled as a path graph, that representation does not expose the maximum-sum invariant and adds no useful traversal decision.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_graph: The output depends on contiguous accumulation, not arbitrary edge membership; quadratic graph storage is irrelevant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tree_rules: A forced tree analogy does not match the optimization state or answer contract.

items.prompt: The input declares all users and friendship pairs. The task asks how many separate friendship groups exist, including users with no friendships. What signal determines the overall traversal shape?
constraints: Each friendship pair {u, v} is an undirected edge.

options.text: Use one parent per user and omit a visited set because friendship groups behave like trees.
Run one BFS from the first listed user; BFS is always faster and will find every group.
Start from every user but count a group only when the start is dequeued, because dequeue marking is equivalent.
The whole vertex set must be scanned, starting a traversal from each still-unvisited user.

feedback.reason: Counting groups requires whole-graph coverage, not a single-source reachable set.

blocks.text: Each unseen outer-loop start identifies one component

items: Initialize every declared user as unvisited, including users with no friendship edges.
When the scan finds an unvisited user, increment the group count once and run BFS or DFS from that user.
Mark the entire reachable friendship group before the outer scan continues.

blocks.text: One traversal from the first user cannot cross into a disconnected group. An isolated user is still found by the outer scan and contributes one component. General friendship graphs may contain cycles, so a static tree-parent model is insufficient; dequeue timing also does not define when a new component begins.

blocks.title: Whole-graph shape
blocks.text: Count one component per unvisited outer-loop start, then exhaust that start's reachable set before continuing.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_source: One traversal reaches only the first user’s component, regardless of BFS speed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mark_on_dequeue: Late marking can admit duplicate frontier entries; the component count is tied to choosing an unseen start before traversal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tree_parent: General friendship graphs can contain cycles; tree traversal rules do not apply unchanged.
